We are just starting so we are still connected to the ISP. This makes us a Tier 2 network (a very tiny one) since we still pay for outside connectivity, but we are all settlement-free among ourselves which we are making mandatory for any new nodes. This means all nodes must agree to carry the traffic of any other node without caps and without money changing hands.

If we continue to grow to a few thousand nodes we might become Tier 1 in the future and stop buying connectivity from an ISP. This would only be possible if the local university and the business district decides to participate. The university is also Tier 2 I believe but the business district are entirely ISP dependent. Becoming a part of Tier 1 network would make them a prime data center location for this part of the city. It would be expensive but it would also double their value.

Ok sounds interesting. I had a cousin doing something similar. Except he was going to be the ISP for a secluded area; through satellite internet I think. Well I'm glad something like this is happening. I love the decentralization aspect of it. What safeguards do you have of preventing someone to inspect all the traffic and steal bank info, etc?

Ok, everything I was talking about so far was on OSI layer 1 and 2 and it is open to snooping. I am a strict proponent that nothing on the internet should be in clear text and everything down to your grandma's shopping list should be strongly encrypted. In our current setup this encryption must happen on higher OSI levels (protocols, encryption etc.) Currently we are not more secure than a standard ISP connection but we are not less secure either, we are about equal. There is room for much improvement though.

If we had 1000 nodes and some clever routing we could make the network very secure against frequency analysis because the node a packet enters the network and the node a packet exits can be quite random. Since the nodes are near each other we can also exchange big keys off channel.

Could you do something like a mini-Tor network separated from the regular Tor network, letting only the nodes connected directly to the outside Internet serve as exit nodes; so things would at least be encrypted while flowing inside your network?
This should be possible though there is no straightforward way of ensuring a node is definitely inside the network since you only have control of your own node.
There is no way for a node inside the network to know whether a node they're connected to is honestly part of the network and not something on the outside?

I can't think of a guaranteed way to do it. Nodes just pass traffic and maintain anonymity. A node only knows about neighboring nodes, not about nodes several nodes across. So you know that a packet is coming from neighbor A but you don't know where neighbor A got it from. This makes it quite secure in a sense because a packet can't be traced.

If you want to make sure you are indeed talking to Joe you must have exchanged a secret with Joe. The network will not do this for you but the usual SSH and similar authentication methods will work. This is not part of the network layout though, it is a different layer on the OSI model. We are mainly talking layer 1 and 2 so far.
Perhaps something like a public web-of-trust stored on a Bitcoin-like blockchain to authenticate nodes without necessarily personally knowing they belong to the network?
How are you peered to get outside traffic?

Currently we don't get outside traffic. We don't even plan to at the current scale of things. We could maybe start thinking of it after we reach 1000 nodes minimum and demonstrate reliable uptime and throughput. Even then we won't be competitive but we are doing this for our own benefit so being competitive won't be a priority. Not having recurring ISP bills would be a good enough advantage for us.

Boy Who Survived Cancer Creates Day Of Kindness (article pasted in comments to avoid ads)

WATERTOWN (CBS) – Shining the light of kindness on a dark anniversary. That’s the goal of a six year old from Watertown. On November 3, three years ago, Gabriel was diagnosed with cancer, but today his hope and enthusiasm have spread around the world.

“Today is Gabriel’s Day of Kindness,” says 1st grader Gabriel Aljalian. He’s healthy and happy now but that wasn’t the case in 2012. “Leukemia,” he says. He endured two and a half years of sometimes painful treatments. “Today, I’m perfect,” he says.

To change this anniversary date of his diagnosis into something good, he invented Gabriel’s’ Day of Kindness. “It means people have to do good stuff,” Gabriel says. Gabriel and his family and friendsare taking gifts to kids at Children’s Hospital and the Dana Farber Cancer Center, and they’ve used social media to ask others to do join in. “There’s acts of kindness in every state in the United States and so many countries around the world, and we’re just overwhelmed,” says Natasha Aljalian, Gabriel’s mother.

One group of family friends made care bags for homeless people and gave them out in Harvard Square Tuesday. “They contain gift cards and socks and warm items and food,” says Maria Derderian, one of the people helping out. One of the people they met was so touched that after she received her package she took an old envelope and wrote Gabriel a thank you note. “I said that I hope he recovers and thank you for caring. And I said you have an angel’s name,” the homeless woman told us.

“Today we’re just counting our blessings and we really want to share that with the world,” Gabriel’s mom says. And for Gabriel, this is just the start. “It’s always nice just to do happy things,” he says.

To find out what people are doing or what you can do: www.facebook.com/gabrielsdayofkindness.
